content.paragraph: To locate a point in a plane, we need two numbers. We know that any point in the plane can be represented as an ordered pair $$(a,b)$$ of real numbers, where $$a$$ is the $$x$$-coordinate and $$b$$ is the $$y$$-coordinate. For this reason, a plane is called two-dimensional. To locate a point in space, three numbers are required. We represent any point in space by an ordered triple $$(a,b,c)$$ of real numbers.

subsection.title: 3D Space
subsection.paragraph: In order to represent points in space, we first choose a fixed point $$O$$ (the origin) and three directed lines through $$O$$ that are perpendicular to each other, called the coordinate axes and labeled the $$x$$-axis, $$y$$-axis, and $$z$$-axis. Usually we think of the $$x$$ - and $$y$$-axes as being horizontal and the $$z$$-axis as being vertical, and we draw the orientation of the axes as in Figure 1. The direction of the $$z$$-axis is determined by the right-hand rule as illustrated in Figure 2: If you curl the fingers of your right hand around the $$z$$-axis in the direction of a $$90^{{^\circ}}$$ counterclockwise rotation from the positive $$x$$-axis to the positive $$y$$-axis, then your thumb points in the positive direction of the $$z$$-axis.

subsection.paragraph: The three coordinate axes determine the three coordinate planes illustrated in Figure 3(a). The $$\mathit{xy}$$-plane is the plane that contains the $$x$$ - and $$y$$-axes; the $$\mathit{yz}$$-plane contains the $$y$$ - and $$z$$-axes; the $$\mathit{xz}$$-plane contains the $$x$$ - and $$z$$-axes. These three coordinate planes divide space into eight parts, called octants. The first octant, in the foreground, is determined by the positive axes.

subsection.paragraph: Because many people have some difficulty visualizing diagrams of three-dimensional figures, you may find it helpful to do the following [see Figure 3(b)]. Look at any bottom corner of a room and call the corner the origin. The wall on your left is in the $$\mathit{xz}$$-plane, the wall on your right is in the $$\mathit{yz}$$-plane, and the floor is in the $$\mathit{xy}$$-plane. The $$x$$-axis runs along the intersection of the floor and the left wall. The $$y$$-axis runs along the intersection of the floor and the right wall. The $$z$$-axis runs up from the floor toward the ceiling along the intersection of the two walls. You are situated in the first octant, and you can now imagine seven other rooms situated in the other seven octants (three on the same floor and four on the floor below), all connected by the common corner point $$O$$ .

Now if $$P$$ is any point in space, let $$a$$ be the (directed) distance from the $$\mathit{yz}$$-plane to $$P$$ , let $$b$$ be the distance from the $$\mathit{xz}$$-plane to $$P$$ , and let $$c$$ be the distance from the $$\mathit{xy}$$-plane to $$P$$ . We represent the point $$P$$ by the ordered triple $$\left( {a,b,c} \right)$$ of real numbers and we call $$a$$ , $$b$$ , and $$c$$ the coordinates of $$P$$ ; $$a$$ is the $$x$$-coordinate, $$b$$ is the $$y$$-coordinate, and $$c$$ is the $$z$$-coordinate. Thus, to locate the point $$\left( {a,b,c} \right)$$ , we can start at the origin $$O$$ and move $$a$$ units along the $$x$$-axis, then $$b$$ units parallel to the $$y$$-axis, and then $$c$$ units parallel to the $$z$$-axis as in Figure 4.

The third line segment, labeled c, begins from the end point of the second line segment, runs parallel to the positive z axis and ends at a point labeled P(a, b, c).

subsection.paragraph: The point $$P\left( {a,b,c} \right)$$ determines a rectangular box as in Figure 5. If we drop a perpendicular from $$P$$ to the $$\mathit{xy}$$-plane, we get a point $$Q$$ with coordinates $$\left( {a,b,0} \right)$$ called the projection of $$P$$ onto the $$\mathit{xy}$$-plane. Similarly, $$R\left( {0,b,c} \right)$$ and $$S\left( {a,0,c} \right)$$ are the projections of $$P$$ onto the $$\mathit{yz}$$-plane and $$\mathit{xz}$$-plane, respectively.

subsection.paragraph: The Cartesian product $$\mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R} = \left\{ \left( {x,y,z} \right) \middle| x,y,z \in \mathbb{R} \right\}$$ is the set of all ordered triples of real numbers and is denoted by $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ . We have given a one-to-one correspondence between points $$P$$ in space and ordered triples $$\left( {a,b,c} \right)$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ . It is called a three-dimensional rectangular coordinate system. Notice that, in terms of coordinates, the first octant can be described as the set of points whose coordinates are all positive.

subsection.title: Surfaces and Solids
subsection.paragraph: In two-dimensional analytic geometry, the graph of an equation involving $$x$$ and $$y$$ is a curve in $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ . In three-dimensional analytic geometry, an equation in $$x$$ , $$y$$ , and $$z$$ represents a surface in $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ .

problem.paragraph: What surface in $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ is represented by each of the following equations?

item.paragraph: The equation $$z = 3$$ represents the set $$\left\{ \left( {x,y,z} \right) \middle| z = 3 \right\}$$ , which is the set of all points in $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ whose $$z$$-coordinate is $$3$$ ($$x$$ and $$y$$ can each be any value). This is the horizontal plane that is parallel to the $$\mathit{xy}$$-plane and three units above it as in Figure 7(a).

subsection.paragraph: Note When an equation is given, we must understand from the context whether it represents a curve in $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ or a surface in $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ . For example, $$x = 2$$ represents a plane in $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ , but of course $$x = 2$$ can also represent a line in $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ if we are dealing with two-dimensional analytic geometry. subsection.paragraph: In general, if $$k$$ is a constant, then $$x = k$$ represents a plane parallel to the $$\mathit{yz}$$-plane, $$y = k$$ is a plane parallel to the $$\mathit{xz}$$-plane, and $$z = k$$ is a plane parallel to the $$\mathit{xy}$$-plane. So the surface $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 1$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ consists of all possible horizontal circles $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 1$$ , $$z = k$$ , and is therefore the circular cylinder with radius $$1$$ whose axis is the $$z$$-axis. problem.paragraph: Describe and sketch the surface in $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ represented by the equation $$y = x$$ .

Solution The equation represents the set of all points in $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ whose $$x$$ - and $$y$$-coordinates are equal, that is, $$\left\{ \left( {x,x,z} \right) \middle| x \in \mathbb{R},z \in \mathbb{R} \right\}$$ . This is a vertical plane that intersects the $$\mathit{xy}$$-plane in the line $$y = x$$ , $$z = 0$$ . The portion of this plane that lies in the first octant is sketched in Figure 12.
